title: Your earnings are ready. First, send money.
subject: Task scam pattern
summary: A supposed job shows earnings, then demands a deposit before you can withdraw them.
lesson: A number on a dashboard does not prove that withdrawable earnings exist. Do not send money to release supposed wages.
message: Great work! Your task balance is now €184. To withdraw it, top up your account with €60 to complete the final task set. The deposit will be returned with your earnings.
counterclaim: €60 deposit requested first
observations: An apparent job offers commissions for simple online tasks.
A displayed balance makes the earnings feel real.
A separate payment is demanded before those supposed earnings can be withdrawn.
source_summary: FTC guidance describes task scams in which an online platform displays apparent commissions, then asks the person to deposit their own money. The message here is an educational reconstruction of that pattern.
limits: The wording and amounts are invented. This is not a victim’s message or an accusation against a named business. A legitimate payout minimum is different from asking someone to send a separate deposit. AI involvement is not established.

title: A lawful-looking request. A disclosure to the wrong party.
audience: Banks, fintechs, legal and compliance teams; affected customers as data subjects
subject: Revolut customer-data disclosure after fraudulent government-domain requests
summary: Revolut confirmed that sensitive customer data was disclosed after fraudulent information requests were sent from a legitimate government-agency email domain.
lesson: For regulated firms, a trusted domain is not enough. Sensitive data requests need independent requester verification, authority checks and escalation paths before records leave the institution.
counterclaim: Requester authority must be independently verified
observations: The reported attack targeted a compliance workflow rather than a public scam landing page.
Revolut told TechCrunch the requests came from a legitimate government-agency email domain and were fraudulent.
Reportedly exposed data included identity and contact details, identity-document copies, and possibly selfies, statements and transaction histories.
Revolut said its systems and customer funds were unaffected, while affected customers were contacted directly.
source_summary: TechCrunch reported on 12 September 2026 that Revolut confirmed a limited number of customers were impacted after fraudulent information requests were sent from a legitimate government-agency email domain. The Block separately reported that the incident involved KYC and account data, with possible Bitcoin transaction history exposure. The Financial Times later reported that nearly 700 customers were affected and that the UK Information Commissioner's Office had opened an investigation.
limits: This case is based on public reporting and Revolut statements quoted by those outlets. The government agency, exact request documents, affected markets and final regulator findings were not publicly established in these sources. The incident should not be described as customer funds being stolen or Revolut's core systems being compromised unless later evidence supports that.
assessment_source: TechCrunch, The Block and Financial Times
